title: Carbon Monoxide Detector Beeping: Causes & Fixes
question: Why is my carbon monoxide detector beeping? Is it a real alarm or just a low battery?
summary: A carbon monoxide detector making a single short chirp every 30–60 seconds is almost always a maintenance signal: a low battery or an end-of-life sensor (CO sensors wear out in about 7–10 years). But a loud, fast, repeating pattern (typically four beeps, a pause, then four more, often with a red light or a spoken "carbon monoxide" warning) means CO may be in your home right now: get everyone and pets outside to fresh air and call 911 from outside. When you cannot tell which sound it is, treat it as a real alarm and evacuate; that error is always the safe one.

commonCauses.cause: A real CO alarm: a loud, fast, repeating pattern (usually 4 beeps, a pause, then 4 more), often with a red light or a spoken 'carbon monoxide' warning. This is NOT the occasional single chirp; it means CO may be present now.
commonCauses.quickCheck: Listen to the pattern: a loud, repeating 4-beep-pause-4-beep cycle (or a voice warning) = treat as real CO. Do not investigate. Get everyone and pets outside and call 911 from outside.

commonCauses.cause: Low battery: a single short chirp every 30–60 seconds. This is a maintenance reminder, not an alarm, and it includes the backup battery in hardwired or plug-in units.
commonCauses.quickCheck: A lone chirp every ~30–60 sec with no loud repeating pattern, often paired with one blinking light, points to a low battery. Swapping the battery (if it is the replaceable type) should stop it.

commonCauses.cause: End of life: CO sensors degrade and expire roughly 7–10 years after manufacture. The unit chirps or announces 'End'/'Err' to tell you to replace the whole alarm, and a fresh battery will NOT stop it.
commonCauses.quickCheck: Take the unit off its bracket and read the manufacture / replace-by date on the back. If it is about 7+ years old, or it keeps chirping after a new battery, it has reached end of life.

commonCauses.cause: Loose, wrong-type, or unseated battery, or a leftover pull-tab or a battery drawer that did not fully close.
commonCauses.quickCheck: Open the compartment: confirm the correct battery type, correct polarity, fully seated, pull-tab removed, and the drawer clicked shut.

commonCauses.cause: A real but transient, low-level CO source: a car warming up in an attached garage, a backdrafting furnace or water heater, a fireplace, or generator fumes drifting inside. This is still real CO, just intermittent, and must never be dismissed as a 'false alarm.'
commonCauses.quickCheck: Did the alarm sound right after starting a vehicle in the garage, lighting a fire, or a fuel appliance kicking on? Ventilate, get out if it keeps sounding, and have the appliance and flue checked.

commonCauses.cause: Dust, high humidity, or a nuisance/malfunction chirp: some units also chirp a distinct error code that varies by brand.
commonCauses.quickCheck: Look for dust around the sensor vents or a very steamy/humid location; check the manual's beep-pattern chart to see if the sound is an error code rather than a low-battery or CO signal.

fixes: First, identify the sound. If it is a loud, fast, repeating pattern (typically 4 beeps, pause, 4 beeps) or a spoken 'carbon monoxide' warning, treat it as a real alarm: get everyone and pets outside to fresh air, call 911 (or your gas utility) from outside, and do not re-enter until the fire department or utility says it is safe. When you cannot tell whether it is an alarm or a chirp, evacuate and verify from outside; that error is always the safe one.

Trust symptoms over the device. If anyone has a headache, dizziness, nausea, drowsiness, confusion, or a flu-like feeling without fever, leave the house and call 911 even if the alarm is only chirping or silent.

If it is a single chirp every 30–60 seconds and no one has symptoms, replace the battery on a replaceable-battery unit: install a fresh battery of the correct type, confirm polarity and that it is fully seated, close the drawer until it clicks, then press and hold the test button to reset.
For a sealed 10-year unit, the battery is not replaceable; a chirp on one of these means end of life, so replace the whole alarm.

Check the date stamped on the back. If the CO alarm is about 7–10 years past its manufacture date, or it keeps chirping after a fresh battery, replace the entire unit; the sensor is spent. Write the install date on the new one with a marker.

Gently vacuum the vents with a soft brush or use short bursts of canned air to clear dust, then re-test. Keep alarms out of very humid, dead-air, or too-close-to-appliance spots (roughly 10–15 ft from fuel-burning appliances) to cut nuisance chirps.

If the chirp followed a car in the garage, a fireplace, or a running fuel appliance, treat it as possible real low-level CO: open windows to ventilate, get everyone out if it keeps sounding, and have the appliance, vent, and chimney inspected by a licensed pro; never assume it was a false alarm.

Never pull the battery or take a CO alarm down just to stop the noise; a disabled CO alarm can be fatal. If you must quiet it while you get a replacement, use the Silence/Hush button (not battery removal) and only after you have confirmed it is a chirp, not a real alarm; then fix or replace it the same day.
Make sure you have UL 2034 CO alarms on every level of the home and near each sleeping area, and replace them on the manufacturer's schedule so a worn-out sensor never leaves you unprotected.
diyVsPro: Diagnosing the sound, swapping batteries, cleaning the vents, reading the date, and replacing a standalone or plug-in CO alarm like-for-like are all safe DIY jobs. The moment the unit sounds a real, repeating alarm, or anyone feels unwell, it stops being a repair and becomes a 911 / gas-utility emergency. And finding or fixing the CO source itself (furnace, boiler, water heater, gas range, fireplace, a cracked heat exchanger, or a blocked flue or chimney) is licensed-pro work for an HVAC or gas tech, often at roof height, and never a homeowner repair.
typicalCostUSD: Battery: $2–$15. Standalone CO alarm: $20–$50; combo smoke/CO ~$40–$70; sealed 10-year unit ~$30–$50. Electrician to replace or add a hardwired/interconnected unit: roughly $100–$250 per alarm, often with a service-call minimum. Finding the source: annual furnace/appliance inspection ~$100–$250; chimney inspection + sweep $150–$400; major combustion/heat-exchanger repair $500–$2,000+. Fire department / gas-utility emergency response: typically free.
timeEstimate: Deciding chirp vs. alarm: seconds, and on a real alarm, evacuate immediately. Battery swap, cleaning, or reset: 5–10 minutes. Replacing a hardwired unit with the breaker off: 20–40 minutes.
safetyNote: A CO alarm's whole job is to warn you before you feel anything: carbon monoxide is colorless, odorless, and can kill. Learn the difference: a loud, fast, repeating alarm (usually 4 beeps, pause, repeating, often with a red light or a spoken "carbon monoxide" warning) means CO may be present RIGHT NOW. Get everyone and pets outside to fresh air and call 911 from outside, and do not re-enter until the fire department or gas utility clears it. A single chirp every 30–60 seconds is only a low-battery or end-of-life reminder. When you cannot tell which it is, treat it as a real alarm and evacuate; that error is always the safe one. If anyone has a headache, dizziness, nausea, drowsiness, or confusion, leave and call 911 even if the alarm is silent. If you also smell gas (a rotten-egg odor), leave immediately and call your gas utility from outside. Never disable or remove a CO alarm to stop the noise, and never troubleshoot a suspected gas or combustion source yourself; that is a job for the fire department, gas utility, or a licensed tech.

Step stool or short ladder (never a chair)
Vacuum with soft brush attachment or a can of compressed air
